newsitem.title: ITALY: UN says one-third of new N.Korea food appeal met.
newsitem.headline: UN says one-third of new N.Korea food appeal met.

text.p: Donors have met almost one third of a new $46 million food aid appeal for starving children in North Korea in record time, a senior U.N. official said on Thursday.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the United Nations food aid agency, the World Food Programme (WFP), told a news conference that the response from donors to an appeal launched officially only on Wednesday had been highly encouraging.
"Already the new appeal has been 31 percent resourced," Bertini said, adding the speed of the response was "unheard of".
"We are confident we will be able to stabilise the situation of North Korea's children and stave off their hunger."
WFP launched the fresh appeal to ease the plight of 2.6 million children under six who are already suffering critical malnutrition as a result of two years of devastating floods.
An appeal earlier this year, for $96 million, has already been covered by donor governments and organisations.

WFP has distributed harrowing pictures and film shot last week of toddlers reduced to skeletons in nurseries and hospitals. Others have bowed legs, the swollen joints of protein deficiency, distended stomachs and badly infected skin sores.

Bertini said the European Commission had pledged $12.8 million in the new appeal, the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) $400,000, Ireland $300,000, Norway $250,000, an Irish charity, Concern Worldwide, $50,000 and U.S. agricultural commodities group Archer Daniels Midland $700,000.
The overall appeal will cover 130,000 tonnes of food, which will take one to three months to arrive and would give children a daily ration of 250g (8.3 ounce) -- some 1,100 kilocalories.
The United States said on Wednesday it was giving the appeal "very serious consideration". A formal answer was expected soon.

The new appeal comes ahead of peace talks with South Korea, China and the United States due to begin in New York on August 5. Analysts say the dire food situation in Stalinist North Korea could encourage compromise and prove a turning point for peace.
But Bertini denied it was a reward for agreeing to come to the negotiating table. "We are not in the rewards business. We are in the business of keeping people alive," she said.
She said the latest appeal would not be the last.
"As far as the rest of the population is concerned, no, this is not enough," she said.
"What we are now seeking to do is to try to create systems where we could reach out to more people in the country...
"If we have these schemes in place then we can ask the international community for additional food for the adult population," she said.
Almost all of North Korea's 24 million people are at risk from the chronic food shortages, which WFP has warned are set to worsen before the harvests in October.

Rolf Huss, a senior WFP official who returned from a mission to North Korea on Monday, said he had seen evidence of severe malnutrition among children in the capital Pyongyang, long protected from the worst of the problem by better food rations than the rest of the country.

WFP operates in eight out of North Korea's nine provinces and Huss said talks were under way to gain access to Ryangang on the Chinese border, which Pyongyang has so far denied, saying the province has been supplied with maize donated by China.
But Huss said talks were underway. "We are confident we will get access fairly soon," he said.
